headline: Seiteki is 静 (sei) plus 的 (-teki).
Umeboshi is 梅 (ume, “plum”) plus 干し (hoshi, “drying, dried”), with hoshi voiced to boshi by rendaku.
Hinata is 日 (hi, “sun”) plus な (na, Old Japanese possessive particle) plus た (ta, “direction, side”).
Asamashii is an adjectivization of the verb 浅む (asamu).
オンライン is from English online.
Gozaimasu is a sound change from 御座ります (gozarimasu, “to exist”, polite form).
Akudoi is first cited to 1694, and its derivation is unclear: perhaps 灰汁 (aku, “lye”) plus どい (doi), or あ (a) plus 諄い (kudoi).
Zatsu, “rough”, is from Middle Chinese 雜 (MC dzop).
Daiben is 代 (dai-, “substitute, in substitution for someone else”) plus 弁 (ben, “speech”).
Yurumu is 緩い (yurui, “loose”) plus む (mu, “-ize, -en”, verbal suffix).
ブーツ is borrowed from English boots.
Kanmuryō is 感 (kan, “emotion”) plus 無量 (muryō, “immeasurable”).
Iede is 家 (ie, “house”) plus 出 (de), the stem of 出る (deru, “to go out, exit”).
モーテル is borrowed from English motel.
Kedamono is literally “thing of hair”: 毛 (ke, “hair”) plus だ (da, genitive marker) plus 物 (mono, “thing”).
Uchikiru is 打ち (uchi, verbal prefix adding euphony or emphasis) plus 切る (kiru, “terminate an action”).
ニュアンス is listed as borrowed from French nuance or English nuance, and is first cited to a 1909 book by Nagai Kafū.
Nayamasu is from Old Japanese, first cited in the Man'yōshū of 759, as the causative of 悩む (nayamu, “to be vexed”).
Shamisen derives from the Okinawan 三線 (sanshin), and was originally called 蛇皮線 (jabisen, literally “snakeskin strings”).
Setsujitsu is 切 (setsu, “keen”) plus 実 (jitsu, “faithfulness”).
Mukuchi is 無 (mu-, “un-”) plus 口 (kuchi, “mouth”).
Kōnetsuhi is 光熱 (kōnetsu, “lighting and heating”) plus 費 (-hi, “expense”).
Saizen is 最 (sai-, “most”) plus 善 (zen, “good”).
Bochi is from the Middle Chinese compound 墓地, literally “grave, tomb + ground, region”, in the kan'on reading.
Otsu, “2nd in rank”, is from Middle Chinese 乙 (MC 'it), and its modern slang sense is an aggressive clipping of お疲れ様です (otsukaresama desu).
タイル is borrowed from English tile.
Gei, “art”, is from Middle Chinese 藝 (“art, skill”).
チャンネル is borrowed from English channel.
Numa appears to be 沼 (nu, “swamp”) plus 間 (ma, “space, area”).
Manugareru is from Old Japanese 免る (manukaru), 目 (ma-, “eye”) plus 抜かる (nukaru, “to mistake”).
